The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\dfrac{2}{3},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta$ as follows:

$$
x = \cos\theta, \qquad y = \sin\theta.
$$

We're given that $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cos\theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sin⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\sin\theta$ is positive in the first quadrant. 

So our final answer is $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt 5}{3}.$

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/52/52fe94bb303a001e89f9db221e9730d4ca8c5c284217aa20fb6084ee041dec66.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=cos⁡\theta ,\,y=sin⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $sin⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =2-2{(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{4})}^{2} \\  & =2-2(\frac{10}{16}) \\  & =2-\frac{20}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So our final answer is $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{4}.$
